lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Pressure and Its Relationship with Force

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Demonstrate the action of pressure through a number of activities, such as using a drinking straw, pumping car tyres, filling balloons, and water jets at washing bays.
- Describe the relationship between pressure and force, and discuss the application of pressure in everyday life.

pages.title: What is Pressure?
pages.body: Pressure is defined as the amount of force acting on a given area, calculated by dividing the force applied by the area over which it acts. This relationship is expressed in the formula pressure equals force divided by area, meaning the same amount of force can produce very different pressures depending on how large or small the area it is spread across happens to be.

questions.q: Pressure is defined as
o: Force divided by area
Force multiplied by area
Mass divided by volume
Mass multiplied by acceleration
questions.e: Pressure is defined as the amount of force acting on a given area, calculated by dividing the force applied by the area over which it acts.

pages.title: How Pressure Relates to Force
pages.body: Since pressure equals force divided by area, a given force produces greater pressure when concentrated over a smaller area, and lower pressure when spread across a larger area. This explains why a sharp knife, which concentrates force over a very small cutting edge, cuts through material far more easily than a blunt knife applying the same force over a wider, duller edge, and why a person wearing snow shoes, which spread their weight over a larger area, sinks less into soft snow than the same person wearing ordinary shoes.

pages.title: Demonstrating Pressure with a Drinking Straw
pages.body: Sucking a drink through a straw demonstrates pressure in action, since sucking reduces the air pressure inside the straw, and the higher air pressure pushing down on the surface of the drink outside the straw then forces the liquid upward into the straw and into the mouth. This everyday activity relies entirely on a pressure difference between the inside and outside of the straw to move the liquid.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Demonstrating Pressure by Pumping Car Tyres

pages.title: Demonstrating Pressure by Pumping Car Tyres
pages.body: Pumping air into a car tyre increases the pressure of the air trapped inside the tyre, since more air molecules are forced into essentially the same enclosed volume, increasing the force those molecules exert against the inside of the tyre wall for every unit of area. A properly inflated tyre, at the correct pressure, supports the vehicle's weight safely and provides good grip on the road, while an underinflated tyre, at too low a pressure, can wear unevenly and handle poorly.

pages.title: Demonstrating Pressure by Filling Balloons
pages.body:
Blowing air into a balloon increases the pressure of the air trapped inside it, causing the balloon's elastic material to stretch outward until the outward pressure from the trapped air balances the inward pull of the stretched balloon material. Continuing to blow more air in raises the pressure further, eventually beyond what the balloon material can safely withstand, at which point it bursts.

[[pic:A four panel illustration, the first panel showing a person drinking through a straw with arrows showing air pressure pushing liquid upward, the second showing a hand pump inflating a car tyre with a pressure gauge reading increasing, the third showing a person blowing up a balloon that visibly expands, and the fourth showing a strong water jet from a hose being used to wash a car at a washing bay, each panel labelled with the relevant pressure concept.]]

Notice how each of these everyday activities, drinking through a straw, inflating a tyre, filling a balloon, and washing with a water jet, relies on creating or using a difference in pressure to achieve a practical result.

pages.title: Water Jets at Washing Bays
pages.body: A water jet used at a car washing bay concentrates a relatively modest force of flowing water over a very small nozzle opening, producing a high pressure jet capable of removing dirt and grime effectively from a vehicle's surface. This is a direct, practical application of the pressure formula, since reducing the area the force acts through, by narrowing the nozzle, significantly increases the resulting pressure.

pages.title: Everyday Applications of Pressure
pages.body: Beyond the activities already described, sharp knives and needles, wide foundations for heavy buildings, and the design of hydraulic systems in machines such as car jacks and braking systems all rely on the same basic relationship between force, area and pressure. Recognising this shared underlying principle across such varied examples highlights how central the concept of pressure is to understanding many aspects of everyday life and technology.

lessons.title: The Unit of Pressure and Worked Examples

pages.title: The Unit of Pressure and Worked Examples
pages.body:
Pressure = force divided by area. Force is measured in newtons, written N, and area in square metres, written m². The unit of pressure is therefore the newton per square metre, written N/m², which is also called the pascal, written Pa. One pascal is a pressure of one newton acting on one square metre.

| **QUESTION** | **WORKING** | **ANSWER** |
|---|---|---|
| **A box of weight 200 N rests on an area of 2 m². Find the pressure it exerts** | Pressure = force divided by area = 200 divided by 2 | 100 N/m², or 100 Pa |
| **The same box is turned so that it rests on an area of 0.5 m². Find the new pressure** | Pressure = 200 divided by 0.5 | 400 N/m². The pressure is four times greater because the area is four times smaller |
| **A pressure of 500 N/m² acts on an area of 3 m². Find the force** | Force = pressure multiplied by area = 500 multiplied by 3 | 1 500 N |
| **A force of 600 N produces a pressure of 300 N/m². Find the area** | Area = force divided by pressure = 600 divided by 300 | 2 m² |

pages.title: Atmospheric Pressure, Pressure in Liquids and Applications
pages.body:
The air around the Earth has weight and presses on everything. This is called atmospheric pressure. It is atmospheric pressure that pushes a drink up a straw when the pressure inside the straw is reduced, holds a rubber sucker on a smooth wall and fills a syringe when the plunger is pulled back. Pressure in a liquid increases with depth, which is why the wall of a dam is thickest at the bottom and why water spurts farthest from the lowest hole in a container. Pressure applied to a liquid in a closed space is passed on equally in all directions, which is the principle of hydraulic brakes and hydraulic jacks.

| **APPLICATION** | **HOW PRESSURE IS USED** |
|---|---|
| **Sharp knives, needles and nails** | A small area gives a large pressure, so they cut or pierce easily |
| **Wide tyres of tractors and broad feet of camels** | A large area gives a small pressure, so they do not sink into soft ground |
| **Foundations of buildings** | A wide base spreads the weight and reduces the pressure on the ground |
| **Water jets at washing bays** | Water forced through a narrow nozzle leaves at high pressure and removes dirt |
| **Car tyres and footballs** | Air pumped in is squeezed into a small space, so it presses hard on the walls and keeps them firm |

🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- State Newton's Third Law of Motion.
- Discuss Newton's Third Law of Motion and show its importance to life.

pages.title: Stating Newton's Third Law of Motion
pages.body: Newton's Third Law of Motion states that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction, meaning that whenever one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object exerts a force of exactly equal size, but in exactly the opposite direction, back on the first object. These two forces, often called the action force and the reaction force, always occur together, act on two different objects, and are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.

pages.title: Understanding Action and Reaction Pairs
pages.body:
An action and reaction pair always involves two separate objects, with the action force acting on one object and the reaction force acting on the other, which is an important distinction, since the two forces never act on the same object and therefore never simply cancel each other out for that object. For example, when a swimmer pushes backward against the water with their hands and feet (the action), the water pushes the swimmer forward with an equal and opposite force (the reaction), propelling the swimmer through the water.

[[pic:A labelled diagram showing a swimmer in water, with one arrow pointing backward from the swimmer's hands labelled Action, swimmer pushes water backward, and a second, equal length arrow pointing forward from the water onto the swimmer labelled Reaction, water pushes swimmer forward, clearly showing the two forces acting on two different objects (the swimmer and the water).]]

Notice that the action force acts on the water, pushing it backward, while the reaction force acts on the swimmer, pushing them forward, illustrating why action and reaction forces, though equal and opposite, do not cancel out for either object individually.

pages.title: The Importance of Newton's Third Law in Life
pages.body: Enabling movement, supporting structures, and explaining the operation of many machines are three broad areas where Newton's Third Law is important to everyday life. Walking itself relies on this law, since a person pushes backward against the ground with their foot (the action), and the ground pushes the person forward with an equal and opposite reaction force, which is what actually propels the person ahead. Similarly, a rocket launches into space by expelling exhaust gases downward and backward at high speed (the action), with the resulting reaction force pushing the rocket upward and forward. Even something as simple as sitting in a chair relies on this law, since your body pushes down on the chair (the action), and the chair pushes back up on your body with an equal and opposite reaction force, which is what keeps you supported rather than falling through the chair.

pages.title: Why Understanding This Law Matters
pages.body: Understanding Newton's Third Law helps explain phenomena that might otherwise seem confusing or counterintuitive, such as why a person can walk forward at all if the ground itself is not visibly pushing them, or why a swimmer or a rocket can move forward by pushing something else backward. This understanding is foundational not only for physics, but for engineering fields that design vehicles, machines and structures that rely on carefully balanced forces to function safely and effectively.

pages.title: Predicting the Outcome of an Action Force
pages.body: Building on Lesson 13, whenever a force (the action) is exerted on an object, that object exerts an equal and opposite force (the reaction) back on whatever exerted the original force. Predicting the outcome of this interaction means recognising, before an activity even begins, that both objects involved will experience a force, that these two forces will be equal in size, and that the two forces will act in exactly opposite directions.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: What Happens When a Force is Exerted on an Object

pages.title: What Happens When a Force is Exerted on an Object
pages.body: When a force is exerted on an object, for example when a person pushes against a wall, that object (the wall) experiences the applied force directly, and, according to Newton's Third Law, immediately exerts an equal and opposite force back on whatever applied the original force (the person). This means the person pushing the wall feels a force pushing back against their hands, even though the wall itself does not appear to move.

pages.title: What Happens as a Reaction from the Object
pages.body: The reaction from the object is the force it exerts back on the original source of the action force, and this reaction force always acts in the direction exactly opposite to the original action force. Importantly, this reaction is not a delayed response, it occurs at exactly the same instant as the action force, since the two forces are simply two aspects of a single physical interaction between two objects.

questions.e: Importantly, this reaction is not a delayed response, it occurs at exactly the same instant as the action force, since the two forces are simply two aspects of a single physical interaction between two objects.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: What Happens When the Force Exerted Equals the Reaction

pages.title: What Happens When the Force Exerted Equals the Reaction
pages.body:
Since Newton's Third Law states that action and reaction forces are always equal in magnitude, whenever we measure the force exerted by one object on another, we can predict with confidence that the reaction force will be exactly the same size, though acting in the opposite direction. This equality holds true regardless of the size, mass, or nature of the two objects involved, whether it is a person pushing a wall, a rocket expelling gas, or a football colliding with a boot.

[[pic:A labelled diagram showing a person pushing against a fixed wall, with an arrow from the person to the wall labelled Action Force (person pushes wall), and an equal length arrow from the wall back to the person labelled Reaction Force (wall pushes person), both arrows drawn the same length to emphasise the equal magnitude of the two forces, alongside a small note explaining why the wall itself does not move despite experiencing a force.]]

Notice that although the wall experiences a real force from the person pushing it, the wall does not move, since it is fixed firmly to the ground and other structures, which absorb the force without the wall itself accelerating, unlike a movable object, such as a skateboard, which would visibly move in response to the same kind of reaction force.

pages.title: Performing an Activity to Justify Predictions
pages.body: Testing predictions about Newton's Third Law can be done through a simple, safe activity, such as two learners of different sizes standing on skateboards or roller skates facing each other, then pushing against each other's hands. Before the activity, predictions can be made about what will happen to each learner, and after performing the activity, observing that both learners move apart, though possibly at different speeds depending on their mass, justifies and refines the original prediction, since the forces are equal but the resulting acceleration and speed of each learner also depends on their individual mass.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

This activity also introduces an important related idea, that while action and reaction forces are always equal, the effect a force has on an object's motion depends on the object's mass as well as the force applied, a relationship studied in more detail in the next lesson through Newton's other laws of motion and the concept of momentum.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Newton's Laws of Motion and Momentum

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Explain Newton's Laws of Motion and relate them to momentum.
- Demonstrate the application of Newton's Laws of motion in everyday life.
- Derive the formula f = ma, where f is force, m is the mass of the object, and a is the acceleration, from Newton's three Laws of Motion, and use the formula to calculate the force a moving mass exerts when moving with a known acceleration.

pages.title: Newton's First Law of Motion
pages.body: Newton's First Law of Motion, often called the law of inertia, states that an object at rest will remain at rest, and an object in motion will continue moving at a constant speed in a straight line, unless acted upon by an external, unbalanced force. This law explains why passengers in a car feel pushed forward when the car suddenly brakes, since their bodies tend to continue moving forward at the car's original speed until a force, such as a seatbelt, acts to slow them down along with the vehicle.

pages.title: Newton's Second Law of Motion
pages.body: Newton's Second Law of Motion states that the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it, and inversely proportional to its mass, meaning a larger force produces greater acceleration, while a larger mass produces less acceleration for the same force. This relationship is expressed in the formula force equals mass multiplied by acceleration, commonly written as f equals m multiplied by a.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Deriving f = ma from Newton's Laws

pages.title: Deriving f = ma from Newton's Laws
pages.body: Newton's Second Law directly gives the relationship between force, mass and acceleration, since the law states that force is proportional to mass multiplied by acceleration, and when a suitable, consistent set of units is used, this proportionality becomes an exact equality, f equals m multiplied by a. This formula allows the force acting on an object to be calculated directly, provided the object's mass and its acceleration are both known.

pages.title: Worked Example Using f = ma
pages.body:
Consider an object with a mass of 5 kilograms accelerating at 2 metres per second squared. Using the formula f equals m multiplied by a, the force can be calculated as f equals 5 multiplied by 2, giving f equals 10 newtons. This means a force of 10 newtons is needed to accelerate a 5 kilogram mass at 2 metres per second squared, and the same formula can be used to solve for mass or acceleration if force and one of the other two values are known instead.

[[pic:A worked calculation diagram showing a labelled trolley of mass 5 kg accelerating at 2 m/s squared, with an arrow labelled Force, and a boxed calculation showing f = m x a, then 5 x 2 = 10 N, clearly presented step by step.]]

Notice how the formula f equals m multiplied by a connects three quantities directly, allowing any one to be found once the other two are known, which is why this formula is one of the most widely used relationships in the study of forces and motion.

pages.title: Newton's Laws and Momentum
pages.body: Momentum is a property of a moving object, calculated by multiplying its mass by its velocity, and it describes how difficult it is to stop or change the motion of that object. Newton's Second Law can also be understood in terms of momentum, since force is related to the rate at which an object's momentum changes over time, meaning a larger force produces a faster change in momentum. Newton's Third Law also connects closely to momentum, since when two objects interact through equal and opposite action and reaction forces, they experience equal and opposite changes in momentum, a principle used to explain collisions between objects such as vehicles or billiard balls.

pages.title: Applying Newton's Laws in Everyday Life
pages.body: Seatbelts in vehicles rely on Newton's First Law, holding passengers in place during sudden stops when their bodies would otherwise continue moving forward. Sports such as football and boxing rely on Newton's Second Law, since a harder kick or punch, applying greater force, produces greater acceleration on the ball or target. Rocket propulsion and swimming, studied in earlier lessons, rely on Newton's Third Law. Together, these three laws provide a complete framework for understanding and predicting how and why objects move, speed up, slow down, or change direction in everyday situations.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Newton's Laws of Motion, though developed several centuries ago, remain fundamental to modern engineering, including vehicle design, structural engineering, and even space exploration, showing how enduring and widely applicable these three relatively simple laws have proven to be across an enormous range of practical situations.
